He runs fixed scope "in a box" GTM, PMM, AEO/SEO, content and partner revenue projects for B2B SaaS and security startups, and sells Claude skills for marketers. Career path

### Career Reflection in a timeline view

Seven years, from a first QA job in Chennai to leading growth at AccuKnox. Select a year to open the rest of it.

May 2020

#### Engineering, QA and AIESEC

Finished a BE in Computer Science at St. Peter’s College, Chennai. Served on an AIESEC exchange in Mansoura, Egypt on the SDG goals, then took a first job as a QA engineer at Visual BI Solutions, raising 100+ bugs on a custom Power BI product.

Jan 2021

#### Joined AccuKnox

Joined as a Project Management Executive at product inception. Worked on the website, product led growth and the v1.0 GA release of the SaaS platform. Started writing on Medium about tech, travel and learning.

Jan 2022

#### KubeArmor Community

Took on community management for KubeArmor, the CNCF runtime security project. Ran campaigns and event planning on the journey from 500K to 1M+, and earned Scrum Master and Product Owner certifications.

Mar 2023

#### Project Manager

Owned the product roadmap and backlog, wrote epics from customer and partner research, and ran the Kubernetes Security Meetup with NetApp for 50+ attendees. Named Employee of the Month in June.

Mar 2024

#### First Product Marketer

Became the founding product marketer. Led GTM for new product lines, built a team of 7 marketers and ran the KubeArmor booth push that added 1.4K+ GitHub stars. Started an MBA at BITS Pilani.

2025

#### Startup of the Year

AccuKnox won the #1 Startup Award at Security BSides Bangalore. The growth team helped take ARR from $500K past $1M, and AI search work put AccuKnox in the Google answer for CNAPP vendors.

Mar 2026

#### Product Marketing and Partnerships Lead

Promoted to lead growth across marketing and partnerships, with $2M in influenced pipeline on $100K a year. Completed the MBA, won BSides again and hosted GrowthX and CNCF community events.

## About Syed Hadi, Product Marketing Lead | Syed Hadi

Hi there

### I’m Syed Hadi.

I lead product marketing and channel partnerships at AccuKnox, a Zero Trust CNAPP and AI security company. I joined in 2021 when the product was still being built and have worked across project management, product, marketing, sales and partnerships since.

I work best with security and SaaS teams past the zero to one stage who need a sharp story, a partner motion and an inbound engine that compounds into ARR. I completed an MBA at BITS Pilani alongside the day job.

How I work

### Human Built Strategy, Powered by AI

Four steps I run on every launch, campaign and partner program.

01

#### Research and positioning
Talk to buyers, partners and sales. Map the competitive field. Land one sharp story the whole company can repeat.

02

#### Build the system
Turn the story into pages, decks, content and the apps and agents that keep the engine running without manual work.

03

#### Launch and enable
Ship it through webinars, events, partners and AI search, then train sales and partners until they sell it better than I do.

04

#### Measure and compound
Tie every motion to influenced pipeline and ARR. Keep what compounds, cut what does not.

See the results this process produced.

## 30 Day Shadow AI Discovery Sprint Plan | Syed Hadi

URL: https://syedcreates.com/30-day-shadow-ai-discovery-sprint
Summary: A 30 day shadow AI risk audit playbook. Discover AI usage, classify data flows, build a risk register and add guardrails without slowing the business down.

Syed Hadi May 12, 2026 · AI security

If I joined a security team tomorrow and someone told me, “We think Shadow AI is everywhere, go figure it out, fast,” I would not begin with a ban.

I wouldn’t send a scary all-hands memo. I wouldn’t publish a giant policy PDF that nobody reads. And I definitely wouldn’t start by assuming employees are the problem.

I’d start with a simple premise: when people adopt AI outside formal approval channels, it usually means the business has moved faster than security, not that the business has stopped caring about security.

That framing matters, because a good shadow AI risk audit is not a witch hunt. It’s a fast, practical exercise in visibility, context, and control. The goal is to find where AI is already being used, understand what data is touching those tools, and put in guardrails that reduce risk without killing momentum.

This is the 30-day playbook I’d use.

### First, I’d define Shadow AI the way the business actually experiences it

In security conversations, “shadow AI” can sound abstract. In practice, it’s much more ordinary.

It looks like:

- A sales rep pasting customer call notes into a public LLM to draft follow-up emails

- An engineer using an unapproved coding assistant tied to a personal account

- A product manager uploading roadmap screenshots into a chatbot for summarization

- A support team experimenting with AI browser extensions that can read ticket contents

- A data analyst connecting internal CSV exports to a third-party AI notebook

None of this is rare anymore. And most of it doesn’t start with malicious intent. It starts with convenience.

That’s why I think teams get Shadow AI wrong when they treat it like classic shadow IT. The pace is faster, the barrier to entry is lower, and the data exposure paths are more subtle. One prompt can include source code, PII, commercial terms, internal strategy, or regulated data. One browser plugin can quietly expand the blast radius.

So my first step would be to align stakeholders on one operational definition:

Shadow AI is any AI tool, model, agent, plugin, or workflow that interacts with company data or business processes outside approved governance.

That definition is broad on purpose. If you define the problem too narrowly, you miss the real risk surface.

### My goal for 30 days would be simple: visibility first, friction second

In a month, I’m not trying to build a perfect long-term AI governance program. I’m trying to answer five questions:

- Which AI tools are actually in use?

- Who is using them?

- What data is flowing into them?

- Which use cases are acceptable, risky, or unacceptable?

- Where do we need immediate guardrails?

That’s it.

If I can answer those five questions with confidence, I can move from vague anxiety to operational control.

### Days 1 to 5: I’d start with AI discovery, not policy writing

The biggest mistake I see is teams starting with policy before discovery. That almost guarantees policy divorced from reality.

In the first week, I would focus on AI discovery across four layers:

#### 1. Network and SaaS visibility

I’d pull outbound traffic and SaaS usage data to identify known AI services, model APIs, browser-based tools, and AI-enabled SaaS apps. This usually reveals more than people expect.

Not just the obvious tools, either. Yes, you’ll find mainstream chatbots. But you’ll also uncover:

- AI meeting note tools

- AI writing assistants

- AI-powered research tools

- AI plugins embedded inside existing SaaS platforms

- Model API calls hidden inside internal apps or scripts

The question I’d ask is not “Do we see ChatGPT?” It’s “What AI-capable destinations are touching corporate identities, endpoints, or data?”

#### 2. Identity mapping

Then I’d map usage to real identities, teams, and business functions.

A raw domain list is not enough. Security needs context. If usage comes mostly from marketing and product, that means one thing. If it comes from engineering and finance, that means something else entirely.

I want to know:

- Which departments are the heaviest users

- Whether people are using corporate or personal accounts

- Whether contractors are in the mix

- Whether privileged users are interacting with external AI tools

This step matters because Shadow AI risk is not evenly distributed. The same tool can be low risk in one team and critical in another.

#### 3. Endpoint and browser telemetry

A lot of Shadow AI lives in the browser. Extensions, local apps, desktop copilots, and side-loaded assistants often escape traditional SaaS reviews.

If I have the telemetry, I’d look for:

- AI browser extensions

- Local AI agents and wrappers

- Unsanctioned plugins tied to email, CRM, docs, or source control

- Clipboard-heavy interactions with sensitive apps

This is where the audit starts becoming real. You stop talking about “AI adoption” as a trend and start seeing specific workflows.

#### 4. Internal interviews with high-probability teams

I would spend time with engineering, sales, support, legal, HR, and data teams before I ever schedule broad awareness sessions.

Not in an interrogative way. More like: “Show me where AI is already helping you. I’m trying to protect the workflow, not shut it down.”

That one sentence changes the tone of the whole audit.

People are far more honest when they think security is trying to preserve productivity instead of policing innovation.

### Days 6 to 10: I’d classify data flows before I classify tools

Here’s a view I feel strongly about: tools don’t create risk in isolation. Data flows do.

A generic chatbot is not automatically high risk. It becomes high risk when employees paste source code, M&A details, patient records, secrets, or customer contracts into it.

So after discovery, I’d build a lightweight map of what data is going where. These are the three categories I’d use.

#### Low-risk usage

Examples:

- Rewriting public marketing copy

- Brainstorming blog titles

- Summarizing non-sensitive public research

- Drafting generic internal communications

These use cases are usually manageable with basic guidelines.

#### Medium-risk usage

Examples:

- Summarizing internal project notes

- Drafting customer communications from CRM context

- Using AI coding assistants on non-sensitive repositories

- Uploading sanitized spreadsheets for analysis

These require controls, approved tools, and clear user boundaries.

#### High-risk usage

Examples:

- Pasting source code from sensitive repos

- Uploading PII, PHI, or financial records

- Sending legal drafts, board material, or unreleased product plans

- Giving AI tools access to internal systems or agentic permissions without review

This is where immediate guardrails need to kick in.

If your teams haven’t already done this exercise, an AI governance checklist helps make classification consistent. At AccuKnox, we’ve seen the same principle play out across cloud and application security too: decisions improve when teams evaluate context, integration paths, and runtime risk together rather than reviewing tools in isolation. That’s one reason I often point people to structured evaluation frameworks like this CNAPP evaluation checklist , not because Shadow AI is identical to CNAPP, but because disciplined security buying and governance follow the same pattern.

### Days 11 to 15: I’d build a simple risk register, not a giant maturity model

At this point, I don’t want a 70-slide strategy deck. I want a working risk register.

For every discovered AI use case, I’d document:

- Tool or model

- Team or owner

- Business purpose

- Data types involved

- Authentication method

- Whether the account is corporate-managed

- Whether prompts, files, or outputs are retained by the provider

- Whether the tool has admin controls, logging, and policy support

- Risk score

- Immediate action: allow, monitor, restrict, replace, or block

This is the moment when the audit becomes operational. You’re no longer discussing Shadow AI as a cultural issue. You’re triaging concrete exposure points.

A practical example:

- Tool. Public LLM via personal account

- Team. Finance

- Use case. Summarizing budget variance narratives

- Data involved. Internal financial performance data

- Risk. High

- Action. Restrict immediately and move the team to an approved AI workspace with logging and retention controls

Another:

- Tool. AI note-taker integrated with Zoom

- Team. Customer Success

- Use case. Call summaries and action items

- Data involved. Customer conversation data, possible contractual details

- Risk. Medium to High

- Action. Review vendor settings, disable external model training, scope meeting permissions, publish approved usage rules

That is the level of specificity that changes outcomes.

### Days 16 to 20: I’d add guardrails where they matter most

This is where most teams either overreact or underreact.

Overreaction looks like blocking every AI domain and calling it governance.

Underreaction looks like writing “don’t paste sensitive data into AI tools” and hoping for the best.

I’d do neither. I’d focus on targeted controls in three areas.

#### 1. Data loss prevention for AI interactions

If you care about data loss prevention for AI, you need more than generic DLP patterns from the email era.

I’d prioritize controls around:

- PII and regulated records

- Source code and secrets

- Contractual or board-level content

- Customer exports and support transcripts

- Internal credentials, tokens, and configuration data

The goal is not to inspect every thought an employee has. The goal is to reduce obvious high-impact leakage pathways.

#### 2. Approved tool pathways

Security teams often underestimate how much risk drops when they provide a good approved alternative.

If employees are using public tools because the sanctioned path is slow, limited, or impossible to access, Shadow AI will keep growing.

I’d establish:

- A shortlist of approved AI tools

- Clear data handling rules for each

- SSO-backed access where possible

- Team-specific guardrails

- Fast review for new requests

This is one area where I think modern enterprise AI security has to evolve. Governance can’t just be a list of restrictions. It needs safe enablement. We’ve written about that shift in our broader guide to AI security and governance , especially the need to connect model risk, data controls, and operational guardrails instead of treating them as separate programs.

#### 3. Runtime controls for high-risk AI workloads

If teams are deploying internal copilots, RAG pipelines, model-serving stacks, or agentic AI systems, I’d go beyond policy and add runtime protection.

This matters because some of the most serious issues with Shadow AI are not just about public chat use. They’re about internal AI systems that quietly inherit excessive permissions, access sensitive datasets, or expose insecure APIs.

The control question becomes: if the AI workflow is compromised, misused, or over-permissioned, what actually stops bad behavior in runtime?

That’s why I think AI governance without runtime enforcement is incomplete. The farther organizations move from “employees using chatbots” to “AI systems acting on enterprise data,” the more they need controls that see and constrain behavior in production. We’ve gone deeper on that in our work around agentic AI security and production-focused AI security monitoring , because this is exactly where theory tends to fail.

### Days 21 to 25: I’d meet teams with findings, not accusations

This part is underrated.

By week four, I would schedule short readouts with department leaders and the heaviest AI-using teams. But I’d present findings in business language:

- Here’s what we found

- Here’s what looks safe

- Here’s what creates real exposure

- Here’s what we recommend changing now

- Here’s the approved path forward

I would not say, “Your team violated policy nine times.”

I’d say, “Your team is clearly getting value from AI, but two of the current workflows create avoidable risk around customer data and unmanaged identities. Here’s how we can preserve the speed without carrying that exposure.”

That framing gets much better adoption.

In my experience, most teams don’t resist guardrails when the guidance is specific, fast, and obviously tied to the way they work.

### Days 26 to 30: I’d finish with a living operating model

At the end of 30 days, I would want six concrete outputs:

- An inventory of discovered AI usage. Not perfect, but materially better than where we started.

- A ranked Shadow AI risk register. With clear ownership and response actions.

- A lightweight acceptable-use policy for AI. Short enough that people will actually read it.

- An approved tools list. Including what data can and cannot be used with each tool.

- Immediate technical guardrails. Especially around sensitive data, unmanaged identities, and risky integrations.

- A repeatable review cadence. Monthly for fast-moving environments, quarterly at minimum for slower ones.

That last point is important. Shadow AI is not a one-time audit problem. It’s a moving target.

New tools appear weekly. Existing SaaS products quietly add AI features. Teams build internal prototypes that suddenly become production workflows. If your audit is static, your understanding is stale almost immediately.

### The biggest mistake I’d avoid: making security the bottleneck

If I had to summarize my philosophy in one sentence, it would be this:

The goal of a shadow AI risk audit is not to stop AI adoption. It’s to make safe AI adoption the easiest path.

That is a very different operating model from traditional security control design.

If you create too much friction, employees route around you. If you offer visibility, approved options, and fast decisions, most teams will choose the supported path.

And honestly, that’s the insider lesson I keep coming back to: Shadow AI is often a symptom of unmet demand.

Teams are telling you they need help writing faster, coding faster, analyzing faster, searching faster, and serving customers faster. Security can either answer that reality with denial, or design controls that work in the real world.

I know which one I’d choose.

### A simple final checklist I’d use

If you need a compact version of this playbook, here’s the checklist I’d personally run:

- Discover all AI-related SaaS, API, browser, and endpoint usage

- Map usage to identities, teams, and business functions

- Classify data flows, not just tools

- Separate low-, medium-, and high-risk use cases

- Build a live risk register with owners and actions

- Add targeted DLP and policy controls for sensitive data

- Provide approved AI alternatives with fast access

- Apply runtime controls to internal AI workloads and agents

- Review findings directly with business teams

- Repeat the audit on a schedule, not as a one-off project

### Conclusion

If I had 30 days to assess Shadow AI, I’d spend less time writing policy and more time finding the truth.

Where is AI already embedded? Which identities are using it? What data is being exposed? Which workflows are worth preserving? Which ones need guardrails now?

That’s the work.

A practical shadow AI risk audit starts with discovery, moves through data and identity context, and ends with controls that are proportionate to risk. Done well, it doesn’t slow the business down. It gives the business a safer lane to move faster in.

And that, in my view, is what good security should do.

## 5 Years of Startup Life: 60 Months, 4 Roles, 1 Journey

URL: https://syedcreates.com/5-years-of-startup-life
Summary: From QA engineer to product marketing lead in five years at startups. The roles, the pivots and the lessons for anyone early in a B2B tech career.

Syed Hadi May 20, 2025 · Career

This day 5 years ago, on May 20, 2020 (in the midst of peak COVID in Chennai), was the first working day of my career! I was a fresh graduate with a curious mind and a job in Quality Assurance at a fast growing startup. Fast forward to today, May 20, 2025, I’m leading global go-to-market strategies as a Product Marketing Manager at a company close to my heart, AccuKnox. These 60 months weren’t just work experience. They were transformation in motion. If you’re in the early stages of your career, this one’s for you.

### The uphill trajectory

#### Year 1. Stepping into the remote corporate

Role. Quality Assurance Engineer. Company. Visual BI Solutions.

My first job wasn’t glamorous, but it was honest work. I was knee-deep in test cases, sanity checks, and bug reports. The product wasn’t just software. It was me. I was building discipline, attention to detail, and the humility to ask, “Why does this matter?”

QA taught me how to think like a user before I ever knew I’d one day lead user-centric marketing.

#### Year 2. The pivot into project management

Role. Project Management Executive. Company. KloudOne.

If Year 1 was about detail, Year 2 was about perspective. I moved from breaking software to building timelines, managing scrums, and steering sprint velocity. I worked across cloud, Kubernetes, and security, learning to listen not just to users, but to teams.

This is when I realised: soft skills build hard products.

#### Year 3. Pressure, product, people

Role. Project Management Executive. Company. AccuKnox.

Joining AccuKnox changed the game. A fast-moving, cloud-native SaaS company, where roles weren’t boxed in. They evolved. I went from project tracking to requirement gathering, from wireframes to GTM strategy brainstorms.

Here, I learned the most underrated corporate skill: ownership. If you see something, build it.

#### Year 4. From projects to strategy

Role. IT Project Manager. Company. AccuKnox.

This phase was a blur of sprints, backlogs, and Product Owner rituals. I wasn’t just driving epics. I was shaping roadmaps. I pitched ideas directly to cofounders, worked across teams, and began leading initiatives that touched real revenue.

I was no longer just part of the engine. I was designing its direction.

#### Year 5. Enter product marketing

Role. Product Marketing Manager. Company. AccuKnox.

In April 2024, I took a bold leap. From execution to storytelling. From sprints to strategy. As a Product Marketing Manager, I now drive global GTM campaigns across 7 regions and 40+ alliances. I lead content, newsletters, analytics, and team members, all while reporting to the C-suite at AccuKnox.

Marketing isn’t just promotion. It’s translation of value, pain points, and potential.

### Lessons from every leap

- QA taught me precision

- Project Management taught me perspective

- Product Marketing taught me narrative

- Every role taught me empathy

### Advice for young professionals

- Don’t rush titles. Chase skills.

- Ask “why” more than “how”

- Say yes to things you’re 60% sure about. The other 40% builds courage.

- Keep a brag doc. You’ll thank yourself during appraisals.

### Why I choose to run a marathon: the AccuKnox chapter

In a world where job-hopping is the norm, I’ve stayed at AccuKnox for over 4.5 years. Not out of comfort, but out of constant challenge.

Here’s why:

- Endless learning. Every quarter brought a new product twist, a new GTM campaign, a new battle to fight. I wasn’t repeating. I was reinventing.

- Exposure to real leadership. I worked closely with the CEO, CTO, co-founders, and seasoned heads of global partnerships. These weren’t just managers. They were mentors in motion.

- Cutting-edge tech. From Zero Trust to Cloud Security, I was hands-on with products that were shaping tomorrow’s security stack.

Internally, I was in rooms I never imagined early in my career:

- Brainstorming with sales, marketing, solutions engineering, and product teams.

- Leading product demos and elevator pitches to both users and executive buyers.

- Managing and enabling channel partners, running alliances training, and collaborating across 7 regions and 40+ partner orgs.

- Onboarding and mentoring freshers and return-to-work professionals, shaping the next wave of talent.

This wasn’t just a job. It became my growth playground.

It’s been a wild ride of learning, pivoting, and growing, with equal parts micro-execution and macro-vision.

### Looking back with gratitude, forward with fire

This wasn’t a straight line. It was a climb. With detours, detachment, and deep learning.

My advice? Your 20s are a sandbox. Build. Break. Iterate. Just don’t pause.

If you’re reading this and feel “stuck,” trust me, growth is closer than you think.

## AEO and SEO Case Study: 27.72% AI Visibility | Syed Hadi

Team results at AccuKnox, a Zero Trust CNAPP and AI security startup, where Syed leads product marketing and partnerships.

The situation

### Where It Started

Security buyers now ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews which CNAPP vendors to shortlist. If a vendor is missing from those answers, it is missing from the deal before sales ever hears about it.
AccuKnox competed with much larger, better funded vendors that already owned the classic SEO results. The team needed a way to show up in both Google and AI answers without outspending them.

- Share of AI answers tracked every week

The lesson. AI answer engines cite pages that answer buyer questions directly. Comparisons, checklists and clear definitions earn citations far more often than product pages.

## How to Evaluate an AI SOC Tool in Regulated Firms

URL: https://syedcreates.com/ai-soc-tool-evaluation-regulated
Summary: Seven tests and a 30 day proof of value for AI SOC tools in banks, healthcare and government, built around evidence, approvals, air gapped deployment and preven

Syed Hadi Jul 21, 2026 · AI security

A polished demo can make almost any AI SOC tool look production-ready.

That is the trap.

In regulated environments, I do not care whether the copilot writes clean summaries, auto-tags incidents, or produces a confident-sounding root cause in 12 seconds. I care whether the tool can stand up to an auditor, preserve evidence, enforce least-privilege, work in an air-gapped enclave, and help my team move from noisy detection to deterministic action.

That changes the whole evaluation process.

If you are buying AI SOC tools for a bank, healthcare provider, insurer, government program, or any environment where incident handling becomes evidence, the demo should be the least persuasive part of the buying process. A slick user interface is easy to tune. Durable controls are not.

### Why regulated buyers should distrust the AI SOC demo by default

Most demos are built for speed-to-wow.

You see natural-language querying. You see auto-triage. You see a chatbot that explains an alert in plain English. Sometimes you see a synthetic attack story stitched together from logs the vendor carefully pre-selected.

What you usually do not see:

- how the model behaves when telemetry is incomplete

- whether every recommendation is explainable and attributable

- what happens when the system is offline from the public cloud

- whether the tool preserves evidence for review

- whether it supports role separation and approval workflows

- whether it can handle AI-specific abuse paths, not just generic SOC narratives

- whether it can stop something, not only summarize it

For regulated SecOps, the question is not “Is this AI impressive?” It is “What control objective does this satisfy, and can I prove it later?”

That mindset filters out a surprising number of demo-first products.

### What changed in the compliance landscape for AI SOC tools

The buying criteria have shifted because the risk model has shifted.

Security teams are now being asked to govern AI systems, not just use AI assistants. That means the operational surface includes model endpoints, prompts, agent actions, dataset exposure, notebook activity, inference paths, service accounts, and policy evidence around all of it. Traditional SOC tooling was not built for that by default.

At the same time, regulated teams increasingly need evidence that is continuous, attributable, and reviewable across cloud, on-prem, hybrid, and isolated environments. That is one reason more buyers are widening evaluations toward platforms that combine runtime telemetry, posture, AI governance, and compliance workflows, instead of relying on disconnected tools alone.

For AI specifically, the bar is now higher than “uses AI for triage.” Buyers need coverage for AI-SPM, AI-DR, Prompt Firewall controls, model and dataset protection, and AI GRC.

### Start with the control objective, not the copilot

This is the first correction I make in every evaluation.

I do not start with feature tours. I start with a control matrix. For each candidate, I ask:

- What operational decision does this tool improve?

- What evidence does it generate?

- What human approvals are preserved?

- What systems of record does it update?

- What can it enforce deterministically?

- How does it behave in my actual deployment model?

For example, “AI explains alerts” is not a control objective. These are:

- reduce false-positive triage time while preserving analyst review

- maintain case history and evidence integrity for incident response

- correlate cloud, identity, runtime, and AI workload events

- detect AI-specific misuse such as abnormal GPU activity or exposed model endpoints

- enforce preventative policy when confidence is established

- operate in on-prem AI SOC and hybrid deployments without depending on outbound SaaS connectivity

Once the control objective is clear, the marketing language gets much less convincing.

### The seven tests I use to evaluate AI SOC tools

I use seven tests. A tool does not need to be perfect in every category. But if it fails two or three of these in a regulated environment, it usually does not make my shortlist.

#### Test 1. Can it explain every alert, summary, and recommendation?

If an AI SOC tool cannot explain its output, I treat it as a drafting assistant, not an operational control.

I want every alert summary, triage recommendation, and remediation suggestion tied back to evidence:

- source telemetry

- detection logic

- correlated entities

- confidence rationale

- time sequence

- analyst-visible provenance

A simple example. If the system says, “Likely privilege escalation attempt tied to suspicious AI workload behavior,” I want to know:

- which identity changed

- which role or permission was granted

- which log source observed it

- which runtime or cloud events were correlated

- why the event was considered abnormal

This matters even more for AI-native SOC workflows because language fluency can hide weak reasoning. Good tools make machine-generated logic inspectable. Weak tools make it look polished.

#### Test 2. Can it preserve evidence, case history, and chain of custody?

In regulated incident response, evidence handling is not optional.

If the AI SOC layer rewrites summaries, collapses case context, or changes earlier findings without preserving history, that is a governance problem. I want immutable or clearly versioned case records, evidence retention controls, analyst actions, timestamps, escalation history, and exportability for review.

This is where many demo-only products start to crack. They look great when generating narrative. They look less convincing when asked to support:

- forensic review

- legal hold

- internal audit sampling

- post-incident RCA

- regulator conversations

- cross-team handoff over multiple weeks

For me, a trustworthy tool behaves like an investigation system, not a chat transcript.

If the vendor also talks about runtime visibility or forensics, I want to see how that links to workload evidence and workload history, not just summarized alerts.

#### Test 3. Can it work with my existing SIEM, XDR, and ticketing stack?

No serious regulated team is ripping out its entire SOC stack because a vendor demo looked smooth.

So one of my fastest screening questions is whether the product can ingest from and export to the systems that already matter. That usually means SIEM, XDR, identity telemetry, cloud control plane logs, case management, and ticketing.

I want to know:

- can it ingest existing detections and enrich them

- can it write back structured outcomes

- can analysts keep using the case workflow they already trust

- can I map AI outputs to existing severity and escalation schemas

- can I keep my evidence in my current system of record

This is where integration depth matters more than the “number of integrations” on a slide. I want field mapping, workflow examples, and failure behavior. If a connector drops, what happens to alert state and case continuity?

#### Test 4. Can it operate in on-prem, hybrid, or air-gapped environments?

This is non-negotiable for many buyers, yet too many demos still treat it like an edge case.

A surprising number of AI SOC tools assume always-on SaaS control planes, cloud-hosted model inference, or external APIs for enrichment. That can be fine for some teams. For others, it is a hard failure.

For air-gapped security operations, I ask the vendor to walk through the architecture without internet assumptions:

- where does model inference occur

- where is telemetry stored

- how are updates delivered

- what breaks if there is no outbound internet

- what deployment options exist for hybrid and isolated enclaves

- what evidence can still be generated locally

That is the difference between a feature and an operating model.

If you serve federal, defense, banking, or healthcare workloads, deployment flexibility is part of product fitness.

#### Test 5. Can it enforce role separation, least-privilege, and human approval?

The fastest way to create risk with an AI SOC product is to give it broad action authority with weak review controls.

In regulated teams, I expect:

- role-based access control

- least-privilege enforcement

- approval gates for high-impact actions

- separation between investigation, recommendation, and enforcement

- auditable action history

- scoped permissions for integrations and service accounts

For example, an AI assistant may suggest isolating a workload, revoking an API token, or blocking a suspicious process. Fine. But who can approve that? Under what circumstances? Is there dual control for sensitive actions? Can the recommendation engine be separated from the enforcement path?

This matters even more when AI meets cloud-native infrastructure. Identity posture, entitlement control, and workload runtime security need to line up.

#### Test 6. Can it handle AI-specific threats, not just generic SOC narratives?

This is where a lot of vendors use “AI SOC” to describe generic SOC automation with a nicer interface.

That is not enough.

If your organization runs LLMs, model APIs, notebooks, agent frameworks, or internal copilots, the SOC needs visibility into AI-specific risks such as:

- prompt injection attempts

- jailbreak patterns

- model endpoint exposure

- insecure plugin or tool invocation

- abnormal GPU consumption

- data exfiltration through prompts or responses

- rogue agent behavior

- model, dataset, and inference tampering

I want to see whether the tool understands the AI attack surface operationally, not just rhetorically. That means evaluating whether it connects AI-SPM, AI-DR, Prompt Firewall controls, red teaming, and AI GRC.

#### Test 7. Can it move from detection to deterministic prevention?

This is the final filter, and the one that matters most to me.

If the tool only explains incidents after the fact, I still have a staffing problem, a dwell-time problem, and a repeatability problem.

The strongest platforms give you a path from detection to prevention, with clear guardrails between observe mode and enforce mode. In cloud-native environments, that usually means policy-driven runtime enforcement tied to real workload behavior, not just another pile of alerts.

This is where a prevention-first architecture stands out. Kernel-level enforcement rooted in KubeArmor and eBPF plus Linux Security Modules is built to move from visibility to controlled enforcement, including staged Audit and Block modes.

[Telemetry] → [Detection/Correlation] → [Explainable Recommendation]
v v v
[Case Record] [Human Approval] [Policy Decision]
v
[Audit Mode → Block Mode]

For me, this is the difference between an assistant and a control plane.

### The red flags that usually reveal demo-only AI SOC tools

These are the patterns that usually tell me a vendor has optimized for theater:

- the copilot is impressive, but the evidence model is vague

- there is no clean answer on where inference runs

- air-gapped deployment gets treated as “roadmap”

- integrations are broad on paper, shallow in workflow reality

- recommendations are not explainable

- actions are not gated by approval and role separation

- AI threat coverage is generic and cloud-security-centric, not AI-workload-specific

- runtime enforcement is absent, or limited to ticket creation and notification

- the product can summarize incidents, but cannot preserve investigation integrity

If I see three of these, I stop being curious.

### A 30-day proof-of-value plan for regulated teams

I prefer a short, structured proof-of-value over a long, charismatic demo cycle.

Days 1 through 5. Define control objectives, success criteria, deployment boundaries, and systems of record. Pick three incident classes to test, for example cloud identity privilege escalation, sensitive model endpoint exposure, and suspicious runtime behavior in a Kubernetes workload.

Days 6 through 10. Connect the minimum viable telemetry set. Do not over-integrate. Use the logs, case workflow, and ticketing path your analysts already rely on.

Days 11 through 15. Run explainability tests. Have the tool summarize real or replayed incidents, then require analysts to validate every summary against source evidence.

Days 16 through 20. Run containment and approval tests. Validate role separation, escalation, human approval, and action logging. In on-prem AI SOC or isolated environments, test degraded-network behavior too.

Days 21 through 25. Run AI-specific threat tests. Use prompt injection, rogue agent behavior, exposed notebooks, or model endpoint abuse scenarios. If the tool cannot reason about those, it is not ready for modern regulated SecOps.

Days 26 through 30. Run the prevention test. Can the workflow graduate from detection and explanation to deterministic policy enforcement, controlled isolation, or preventive runtime action?

If not, you may have found an assistant. You have not found a resilient SOC control.

### What a strong shortlist looks like before you schedule a demo again

A strong shortlist for regulated buyers usually has these traits:

- explainable AI outputs with evidence provenance

- durable case history and chain-of-custody support

- practical interoperability with SIEM, XDR, identity, and ticketing

- support for hybrid, on-prem, and air-gapped security operations

- least-privilege controls, approval gates, and role separation

- coverage for AI-specific threats through AI-SPM, AI-DR, Prompt Firewall, and governance layers

- a credible path from detection to prevention

That last point matters most.

I do not want an AI SOC tool that merely narrates failure better. I want one that helps my team reduce exposure, prove control, and prevent repeat incidents under production conditions.

That is why I evaluate AI SOC tools backwards from the demo. I start with audit pressure, evidence requirements, deployment constraints, and prevention outcomes. Then I ask whether the product can actually survive that reality.

Most cannot.

The few that can are worth a second meeting.

## 7 Runtime Security Questions Before Buying AI-SPM

URL: https://syedcreates.com/ai-spm-7-runtime-security-questions
Summary: Seven runtime security questions that separate AI-SPM platforms that stop threats from ones that only report them, covering agents, Kubernetes and air gapped de

Syed Hadi Jun 10, 2026 · AI security

A lot of buyers are evaluating AI-SPM platforms the same way they evaluated early CSPM tools: connect accounts, discover assets, surface misconfigurations, export a report, feel productive.

I think that’s a mistake.

I work at AccuKnox, and from where I sit, the market is already drifting toward a familiar trap: treating visibility as protection. Discovery matters. Posture management matters. Governance absolutely matters. But if your AI security platform stops at “we found the issue,” then it’s not built for the environments most enterprises are actually running now: agentic workflows, model gateways, Kubernetes-hosted inference, private AI deployments, internal APIs, and data paths that change faster than policy reviews can keep up.

That’s why I wouldn’t buy an AI-SPM tool until it gave me credible answers to seven runtime security questions.

Not marketing answers. Not architecture-slide answers. Real answers.

Because in production, the difference between “we saw it” and “we stopped it” is the whole game.

### Why I’m skeptical of AI-SPM demos

Most AI-SPM demos are polished in exactly the same way: they show model inventory, shadow AI discovery, risk scoring, policy dashboards, maybe some compliance mapping, and a few screenshots of prompt inspection. On paper, that sounds comprehensive.

But I’ve learned to ask a blunt follow-up: what happens when the model, agent, container, or API is already running and doing the wrong thing?

That’s the moment that separates a nice control plane from an actual security system.

In one internal discussion not long ago, we were reviewing how enterprises are adopting AI applications across cloud and private environments. The pattern was obvious: security leaders want governance, but platform teams want something far more practical. They want to know:

- Can this tool work in Kubernetes?

- Can it protect self-hosted models?

- Can it govern agents, not just prompts?

- Can it operate in regulated or air-gapped environments?

- Can it enforce policy at runtime without breaking the application?

That is a very different buying motion from “show me the dashboard.”

If you’re in the middle of an evaluation, here are the seven questions I’d use.

### 1. What exactly do you protect at runtime: prompts, models, agents, containers, or all of the above?

This is the first disqualifier because a surprising number of vendors talk broadly about AI security while protecting only one slice of the problem.

Some inspect prompts. Some monitor SaaS model usage. Some focus on data discovery. Some do model scanning. Those can all be useful. But AI runtime security is broader than prompt filtering.

In practice, enterprise AI risk shows up across multiple layers:

- the model endpoint

- the application calling it

- the agent framework orchestrating actions

- the container or VM hosting inference

- the Kubernetes environment underneath

- the secrets, tokens, and data stores connected to it

If a vendor cannot tell you clearly which runtime layers they can observe and which they can enforce on, you’re not buying a platform. You’re buying a partial feature set.

This is one reason I think the market is moving toward convergence between AI-SPM, CNAPP, runtime protection, and API security. If your AI workloads sit inside your cloud stack, your controls can’t remain logically separate forever. We’ve written about this broader convergence in our guide on what AI security actually means across training, deployment, and runtime .

My rule of thumb. If the answer sounds like “we secure AI” but the architecture really means “we inspect traffic to third-party LLMs,” I move on.

### 2. Can you enforce policy in-line, or do you just generate findings after the fact?

This is where a lot of evaluations become uncomfortable.

Plenty of platforms are good at telling you what happened yesterday. Fewer are built to influence what happens now.

I always ask whether the platform can do any of the following in production:

- block malicious or policy-violating prompts in-line

- prevent sensitive data from leaving approved boundaries

- stop unauthorized agent actions

- isolate compromised workloads

- enforce network or system-level controls around AI services

- apply runtime policy without waiting for human review

If the answer is “we generate alerts and integrate with your SOC,” that’s not nothing, but it’s also not runtime defense.

There’s an old security habit of overvaluing detections because they look measurable in a dashboard. The problem is that AI systems create a lot of fast-moving, chained behavior. By the time a ticket exists, the agent may already have queried an internal system, exfiltrated a response, called an external tool, and written bad data back into a workflow.

That’s why I place so much value on enforcement. In our own AI security work, we’ve leaned hard into the distinction between posture and action, especially around prompt firewalling, policy enforcement, and runtime detection-and-response. If you want a sense of that runtime-first lens, our post on agentic AI security goes deeper.

### 3. How do you govern agent behavior, not just model usage?

This may be the most important question on this list.

Traditional AI security conversations still assume a user sends a prompt and a model sends a response. That’s already outdated for many enterprise deployments. Increasingly, we’re seeing systems where agents:

- retrieve internal data

- call tools and APIs

- take actions across SaaS systems

- trigger workflows

- hand off tasks to other agents

- operate with varying degrees of autonomy

At that point, the security challenge is not just “is this prompt malicious?” It becomes:

- what is the agent allowed to do?

- what identity does it operate under?

- what tools can it invoke?

- what data can it access?

- what actions require approval?

- how do we detect deviation from expected behavior?

If an AI security platform has no serious answer for agent governance, then I’d argue it’s already lagging the enterprise reality.

This matters even more in environments where AI agents are tied to internal APIs, Kubernetes services, ticketing systems, or code repositories. In those cases, an over-permissioned agent starts to look less like a chatbot problem and more like a machine-speed insider risk problem.

In plain English: if the vendor only talks about prompt injection, they’re solving yesterday’s version of the problem.

### 4. Do you support self-hosted, on-prem, and air-gapped AI deployments, or only SaaS visibility?

I’m opinionated on this one because too many teams still underestimate deployment constraints.

A huge amount of enterprise AI experimentation is happening outside clean, internet-native SaaS designs. Some of it is in managed cloud platforms, sure. But a lot of it is also happening in:

- private VPCs

- Kubernetes clusters

- regulated healthcare and financial environments

- sovereign deployments

- defense and public sector environments

- on-prem GPU infrastructure

- partially or fully air-gapped environments

If your shortlist includes vendors that only work when telemetry is sent back to their cloud, that may eliminate them immediately for a regulated buyer.

This is where on-prem AI security stops being a niche requirement and becomes a strategic filter. A platform that cannot meet your deployment model isn’t a weaker option. It’s a non-option.

I’d ask very directly:

- Can you deploy the control plane privately?

- What breaks in an air-gapped environment?

- Which runtime controls still work on-prem?

- Can you protect self-hosted inference engines and local model serving?

- How do you handle hybrid environments where some AI runs in SaaS and some doesn’t?

These questions tend to cut through a lot of vague positioning very quickly.

### 5. How do you secure Kubernetes-hosted AI workloads and the infrastructure around them?

Here’s something I think buyers should say out loud more often: many “AI security” tools are still strangely detached from the infrastructure AI actually runs on.

If your models, APIs, vector services, gateways, and orchestration components live in Kubernetes, then the AI layer and the cloud-native layer are inseparable in practice. You can’t credibly assess risk while ignoring the runtime substrate.

When I evaluate vendors, I want to understand whether they can handle:

- container and workload identity

- process and file behavior

- east-west network controls

- service communication paths

- Kubernetes misconfigurations

- runtime drift

- unauthorized binaries, shells, or outbound connections

- correlation between AI assets and the workloads hosting them

This is one reason I think buyers should look beyond narrow category labels. If an AI-SPM vendor treats Kubernetes as someone else’s problem, you may be left stitching together posture data in one place and runtime reality in another.

That gap creates operational friction, alert fatigue, and blind spots during incident response.

We’ve made this point from the CNAPP side as well: posture without runtime context is incomplete. Our piece on secure AI workloads explores that build-to-runtime connection in more detail.

### 6. What evidence can you produce for policy, risk, and compliance teams?

Security buyers sometimes treat governance as the “non-technical” part of AI security. I think that’s lazy thinking.

In real enterprises, governance is where deployments either scale or stall.

An AI posture management platform should absolutely help answer questions like:

- Which models are approved?

- Where is sensitive data flowing?

- Which business units are using unapproved AI services?

- What controls exist around prompts, outputs, and agent actions?

- Which safeguards are mapped to internal policy or external frameworks?

- Can we generate audit evidence without manual spreadsheet theater?

But here’s the catch: evidence is more meaningful when it reflects enforceable reality, not just intended configuration.

I trust a platform more when it can tie policy to actual runtime behavior, not merely to static settings. For example, it’s one thing to declare that model access is restricted. It’s another to show the agent identity, the attempted action, the violated rule, and the enforcement event.

That is a much stronger story for CISOs, auditors, and risk teams.

If I’m buying for a regulated environment, I want proof, not posture poetry.

### 7. What happens when your platform fails, lags, or loses visibility?

This is the question vendors least enjoy, which is exactly why I ask it.

Security teams are often sold as if controls are omniscient and uninterrupted. Real systems are messier. Sensors fail. Integrations break. Agents evolve. New model endpoints appear outside approved processes. Clusters drift. Teams route around controls to ship faster.

So ask the ugly questions:

- What are your blind spots?

- What dependencies do you have on third-party APIs or cloud telemetry?

- What happens when a workload goes unmanaged?

- How do you detect coverage gaps?

- Can policies fail closed where necessary?

- What backup controls exist if inspection is bypassed?

- How quickly can new AI assets be discovered and classified?

A mature vendor will answer these directly.

An immature one will pivot back to the dashboard.

That tells you a lot.

### The pattern I look for in strong AI-SPM platforms

If I step back, the strongest platforms usually share a few characteristics:

They connect posture to runtime. Not just asset discovery. Not just misconfiguration scanning. They tie findings to what the workload, model, or agent is actually doing.

They understand agentic systems. Not only prompts and models, but tool use, action paths, identity boundaries, and approval logic.

They fit enterprise deployment reality. Cloud, hybrid, private, regulated, and on-prem are treated as first-class requirements, not edge cases.

They reduce operational sprawl. The best solutions don’t force teams to bolt together five disconnected products just to answer one investigation.

If you’re comparing options, the AccuKnox AI security platform roadmap and coverage overview is useful for understanding how these layers are converging across AI-SPM, AI-DR, governance, and runtime controls.

### My bottom line

I’m bullish on the category. I think AI-SPM is real, necessary, and only going to become more important.

But I’m also wary of how fast categories get diluted.

We’ve seen this before in cloud security: a market forms around visibility, then buyers discover that visibility alone doesn’t change outcomes, and then everyone rushes back asking for enforcement, runtime context, and integrated controls they should have demanded from day one.

That’s where I think we are with AI-SPM platforms right now.

So if I were buying today, I wouldn’t start with feature grids. I’d start with disqualifying questions:

- What do you actually protect at runtime?

- Can you enforce, not just detect?

- Can you govern agents, not just models?

- Can you operate in on-prem and air-gapped environments?

- Can you secure Kubernetes-hosted AI infrastructure?

- Can you produce evidence that matters to governance teams?

- What happens when visibility breaks?

If a vendor can answer those well, I’m interested.

If not, I don’t care how elegant the dashboard looks.

Because once AI moves from pilot to production, the prettiest posture report in the world will not stop a rogue agent, a leaking prompt flow, an exposed model endpoint, or a compromised workload.

And that’s the standard I think buyers should hold the market to.

### How Do You Get Your Brand Cited by ChatGPT and Gemini?

Quick answer Answer engines cite brands they can identify and trust. Declare your organisation with schema, keep facts consistent across your site, LinkedIn and directories, answer buyer questions directly in the first lines of a page, allow AI crawlers and earn mentions on sites the models already read.

#### How to use it

- Answer 10 questions About entity data, content, crawl access and third party mentions.

- Read the gaps Each unanswered signal is a concrete fix.
- Verify with the SEO and AEO score Run your URL through the checker to confirm the technical items.

#### The formula
Score = points earned ÷ (10 questions × 2 points) × 100

#### Worked example
Answering 6 questions with full marks and 4 with partial marks earns 16 of 20 points, a score of 80.

#### More questions people ask

##### What is AI visibility?
AI visibility is how often answer engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews mention or cite your brand when buyers ask about your category.

##### How do I check if ChatGPT mentions my brand?
Ask it the questions your buyers ask, such as best tools for your category, in a fresh chat and note whether and how you appear. Repeat monthly with the same prompts.

##### Does schema markup help AI visibility?
Yes. Organization, Person, FAQ and Article schema give answer engines clean facts to quote and help them resolve your brand as an entity.

##### How long does it take to improve AI visibility?
Technical fixes show up within weeks of a recrawl. Third party mentions and authority take months, which is why they are worth starting now.

## ASPM Evaluation Guide: Cut False Positives | Syed Hadi

URL: https://syedcreates.com/aspm-evaluation-cutting-false-positives
Summary: The seven things I would score in any ASPM evaluation when the real goal is fewer, better findings and faster remediation, plus the demo questions to ask.

Syed Hadi Jul 22, 2026 · Application security

If I were buying an ASPM platform today, I would not start with the feature grid vendors want me to compare.

I would start with a harder question:

Will this platform help my team trust fewer, better findings, and move them through remediation faster?

That question matters because most AppSec teams do not have a scanning problem anymore. They have a signal problem. SAST, DAST, SCA, IaC scanning, secrets detection, container scanning: most teams already run multiple tools. The pain hits later, when those tools dump thousands of findings into dashboards and ticket queues that engineering teams stop taking seriously.

I work at AccuKnox, and one thing I have learned from conversations with security leaders is that “more coverage” sounds good right up until your developers are triaging duplicates from five scanners, arguing about exploitability, and reopening the same class of issue every sprint. That is when application security posture management stops sounding like a category label and starts becoming useful.

If my real goal were ASPM platforms reducing false positives, here is exactly how I would evaluate them.

### First, I’d redefine the problem correctly

False positives are not just “wrong findings.”

That is too narrow. In real programs, the pain usually comes from four different sources:

- Literal false positives. The scanner is simply wrong.

- Duplicate findings. Five tools identify the same issue in slightly different language.

- Context-free findings. The issue is technically valid, but low-risk in the actual application path.

- Unactionable findings. The issue is real, but the team has no idea who owns it, where it lives, or what fix should come first.

This is why I think many buyers evaluate ASPM the wrong way. They compare integrations, dashboard widgets, and reporting templates before asking whether the platform improves trust in findings.

For me, an ASPM platform is useful only if it helps answer three questions fast:

- Is this finding real?

- Does it matter in this application’s current context?

- Can the right team fix it without extra detective work?

If the product cannot improve those three outcomes, it is just another place to collect noise.

### My litmus test: does the platform produce one believable story per risk?

This is the first live demo test I would run.

I would give the vendor a realistic environment: maybe one microservice-based application, a couple of repos, one Kubernetes deployment, a CI/CD pipeline, and findings coming from SAST, SCA, secrets scanning, and container scanning.

Then I would ask them to show me a single risk story. Not just a list of alerts. A story.

For example:

“This exposed Java dependency is present in repo A, built into image B, deployed in namespace C, reachable through service D, and owned by team E. It is internet-facing, exploitable under current runtime conditions, and the fix is to upgrade from version X to version Y.”

That is what I want.

If all I get is a normalized findings table with severity filters, I am not impressed. Aggregation is easy. Correlation is hard.

That is why I frame the evaluation around unified context. Modern teams need visibility beyond isolated scanners, especially when they are trying to connect build-time and runtime reality.

### The 7 things I would score in any ASPM evaluation checklist

Here is the practical scorecard I would use.

#### 1. Deduplication quality

Every vendor says they reduce noise. I would want to see how.

Ask:

- How do you merge findings from SAST, DAST, SCA, IaC, API, and secrets tools?

- Do you deduplicate by CVE only, or also by asset, package, code location, exploit path, and business context?

- Can the platform collapse multiple scanner outputs into one remediation item?

This matters because teams do not fix “findings.” They fix issues in systems they own.

A weak ASPM product will show 14 alerts for the same root problem. A strong one will show 1 issue with 14 corroborating signals.

That difference sounds cosmetic until you realize it drives ticket volume, SLA tracking, executive reporting, and developer trust.

#### 2. Reachability and exploitability context

This is where serious false positive reduction starts.

If a platform does not evaluate whether vulnerable code is reachable, whether a package is actually invoked, or whether the service is exposed in practice, it is still prioritizing mostly on static severity.

Static severity alone is a trap.

I have seen teams burn cycles on “critical” findings in dead code while a medium-severity issue in a public-facing API sat untouched because it looked less urgent in the scanner output.

So I would ask:

- Do you support reachability analysis?

- Do you correlate findings with internet exposure or runtime usage?

- Can you combine scanner results with runtime signals or deployment metadata?

- Do you distinguish “present” from “practically exploitable”?

At AccuKnox, we have spent a lot of time thinking about build-to-runtime correlation, because risk gets much clearer when posture is connected to what is actually running in production.

#### 3. Ownership mapping

This is underrated.

You cannot reduce remediation friction if the platform cannot answer: who owns this?

In a modern environment, the same issue may touch:

- a repo owner,

- a service owner,

- a platform team,

- a cloud team,

- and an application team.

If ownership is not mapped automatically, the burden shifts back to the security team. Then your ASPM product becomes another manual routing problem.

I would test for:

- repository-to-service mapping,

- asset tagging,

- business application grouping,

- team ownership assignment,

- ticket routing logic,

- and support for environments where ownership is messy rather than perfect.

A good demo should show me how a finding lands with the right team without a security engineer acting like a human API gateway.

#### 4. Remediation guidance that is actually usable

Here is my cynical view: a lot of “AI-powered remediation” still reads like polished filler attached to a scanner alert.

I would evaluate remediation help very practically.

Can the platform tell me:

- the exact vulnerable package or code path?

- the safe target version?

- whether there is a known fix available?

- whether compensating controls exist?

- whether a fix will break other dependencies?

- how similar issues have been resolved before?

The best remediation guidance removes ambiguity. It does not just add explanation.

For example, “High severity deserialization issue detected” is not helpful.

This is helpful: “Package X in service Y is vulnerable in versions below 4.2.1. The vulnerable function is reachable through endpoint /api/export. The owning team is Payments. Upgrade path has no breaking changes based on dependency graph analysis.”

That is the level of specificity I would want before I believe the platform reduces false positive workload in practice.

#### 5. Workflow fit inside developer reality

This is where many evaluations become theater.

A vendor can demo a polished risk dashboard and still fail in a real engineering organization if the workflow ends there.

Security teams do not close findings. Developers do.

So my ASPM evaluation checklist would include questions like:

- Does it integrate cleanly with Jira, ServiceNow, GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, or whichever systems the team actually uses?

- Can it suppress duplicates without losing audit history?

- Can findings be grouped into one fix ticket?

- Can I push remediation into pull request flows?

- Can I set policy gates without overwhelming pipelines?

- Can teams document accepted risk and exceptions cleanly?

If I have to ask engineers to live in yet another security console, adoption will drop fast.

One thing I tell buyers is simple: tool quality is only half about detection. The other half is behavioral design. The platform has to fit how work already moves.

#### 6. Tuning and suppression controls

No serious buyer should skip this.

Even the best platforms need tuning. Different organizations have different threat models, coding standards, compensating controls, and tolerance for noise. A product that claims to eliminate false positives without tunability is, in my experience, overselling.

I would ask:

- Can I suppress findings with expiration dates?

- Can I suppress globally, by repo, by asset group, or by policy?

- Is there role-based control over who can suppress what?

- Is suppression auditable?

- Can I create environment-specific rules?

- Can I mark findings as “known but accepted” without losing visibility?

This matters even more in regulated environments, where exceptions need to stay visible to both security and compliance teams.

A mature platform should let you reduce noise without creating blind spots.

#### 7. Reporting that reflects real risk reduction, not just finding counts

This might be my biggest pet peeve.

I have seen security dashboards where success is measured by total findings discovered. That is not success. That is inventory.

What I would want instead:

- duplicates eliminated,

- mean time to triage,

- mean time to remediation,

- exploitable findings reduced,

- internet-exposed severe issues reduced,

- reopened findings rate,

- team-by-team remediation performance,

- and trend lines showing posture improvement over time.

If an ASPM tool helps me close 500 meaningless alerts, that is less valuable than helping me close 20 real, high-confidence risks that affect production systems.

The point is not to look busy. The point is to become more credible.

### The demo questions I’d ask every vendor

If I were running a buying process tomorrow, I would ask these directly:

- Show me how you merge findings from multiple scanners into one remediation object.

- Show me how you determine reachability or exploitability.

- Show me how a developer knows this issue belongs to their team.

- Show me how to suppress noise without hiding real risk.

- Show me how this finding becomes a ticket or PR task.

- Show me what changes between a raw scanner alert and a prioritized ASPM issue.

- Show me metrics proving remediation got faster or more accurate after deployment.

I say “show me” intentionally.

I do not want answerware. I want workflow evidence.

### My personal rule: beware platforms that are broad but shallow

This is probably the most opinionated part of my view.

I am cautious of platforms that claim to do everything but cannot go deep on correlation logic. In AppSec, breadth is easy to market because buyers love the idea of consolidation. But if consolidation just creates one giant alert bucket, you have not solved the actual problem.

A platform can ingest SAST, DAST, SCA, secrets, containers, APIs, and IaC findings and still fail the most important test: does the security team trust what rises to the top?

That is why I would rather buy a platform with strong normalization, ownership mapping, and remediation workflows than one with 40 loosely connected modules.

In practice, teams remember one thing after rollout:

Did the platform make life quieter and clearer, or just busier and prettier?

### What good looks like in the first 90 days

If an ASPM deployment is working, I would expect to see some concrete outcomes in the first quarter:

- fewer duplicate tickets reaching engineering,

- better agreement between AppSec and developers on what is worth fixing first,

- shorter triage cycles,

- more confidence in severity,

- cleaner ownership routing,

- better reporting to leadership on actual risk reduction.

I would not expect magic. False positives never fully disappear. But I would expect a noticeable improvement in the ratio of noise to action.

That ratio matters more than almost any product claim.

### Final thought: I wouldn’t buy an ASPM platform to “see more”

I would buy it to argue less.

Less argument about whether a finding is real.

Less argument about whether it matters.

Less argument about who owns it.

Less argument about what to fix first.

That, to me, is the real value of application security posture management.

So if I were evaluating vendors today, my scorecard would stay simple:

Does this platform help my team trust fewer, better findings?

Because once trust goes up, remediation speed usually follows. When remediation speed rises, security starts to feel like part of engineering momentum instead of a tax on it.

That is the standard I would use. Honestly, it is the only one I think matters.

## Best GTM Consultants for Security Startups: How to Choose

URL: https://syedcreates.com/best-gtm-consultants-for-security-startups
Summary: How to choose a GTM consultant for a cybersecurity startup. A six point scorecard, four types of GTM help, red flags and questions to ask.

Short answer. The best GTM consultant for a security startup has sold to technical buyers, ships the work instead of only advising, measures everything in pipeline and understands partner led markets and AI search. Use the scorecard below to compare options.

The scorecard

### Six Things to Look For

01 Has sold to security buyers CISOs, platform teams and DevSecOps leads buy differently from marketing or HR buyers. Ask for deals they influenced with technical buyers.

02 Writes and ships, not only advises You want positioning documents, pages, decks and sequences, not a strategy deck for someone else to execute.

03 Measures in pipeline Every motion should report into sourced or influenced pipeline. Sessions and followers are inputs, not outcomes.

04 Understands channel and partners Many security deals run through distributors, resellers and MSSPs, especially in India, MENA and APAC.

05 Knows AI search Buyers now shortlist vendors in ChatGPT, Gemini and AI Overviews. Your consultant should know how to earn those citations.

06 Hands over a playbook On the last day you should own every plan, sequence and dashboard, with a playbook your team can run.

Your options

### Four Types of GTM Help

Fractional GTM or PMM lead Best for a plan and momentum in 90 days. One senior person writes, ships and coaches your team. Security marketing agency Best for volume in one channel, such as paid media or content production, once your story is clear. Freelance specialist Best for a narrow task, such as a website rewrite or a single launch, with a strong internal owner. Full time head of marketing Best once the motion is proven and you need a daily owner. A fractional lead can help write the role.

Red flags

### Walk Away If You See These

- Promises a fixed number of leads before seeing your data
- No examples of work with technical or security buyers
- Strategy decks only, with no assets shipped
- Reports vanity metrics instead of pipeline
- Wants a long lock in before showing results

Where I fit

### GTM for Security Startups

I lead product marketing and partnerships at AccuKnox, a Zero Trust CNAPP and AI security startup. The team grew sessions 240% in 90 days, reached 27.72% AI visibility and built partner programs across $35B of TAM. I run the same playbook for other startups as GTM in a box .

Schedule meeting Take the GTM health check

Free audit

### Get a free GTM audit of your website.

Share your site and the one thing that is not working. I record a short Loom walkthrough with the three changes I would make first. No call needed.

- Positioning and messaging check
- Conversion and CTA review
- SEO and AI search quick wins

FAQ

### Common Questions

What does a GTM consultant do for a security startup? A GTM consultant defines the ICP and positioning, builds the outbound, inbound and partner motions, and sets up pipeline tracking so you can see which motion produces revenue.
Should a security startup hire a GTM consultant or a full time marketer? Hire a consultant when you need a plan and momentum within a quarter. Hire full time once positioning is proven and the work is steady enough for a daily owner.
How long does a GTM engagement take? Most engagements run 30, 45 or 90 days. The first 30 days cover diagnosis and positioning, and the rest builds and runs the pipeline motions.

## BMI Calculator India: Asian Cut Offs and Healthy Habits Plan

URL: https://syedcreates.com/bmi-calculator
Summary: BMI with Indian cut offs, waist to height ratio, optional BP, sugar and SGPT checks, a start and stop doing plan and a 7 day habits tracker. Free PDF.

BMI - See the plan

Your BMI -

18.5 23 25 30

Healthy weight for you -

Waist to height -

Your first goal -

The PDF includes your start and stop table, any report readings and a printable 7 day tracker.

Your plan

### What to Start, What to Stop

Built from your BMI, waist, habits and any readings you added. Each row says why it matters for you, not for an average person. Change an input above and the table updates.

#### Your report readings

Healthy habits tracker

### Seven Days, Eight Habits

Picked from your plan. Tick a box each day you hit the habit. Ticks are saved on this device only and reset every Monday, so each week starts clean.

0%

Move: 150 minutes a week

Eat: half the plate vegetables

Lift: two strength days

How it works

### The Rules Behind the Numbers

BMI. Weight in kg divided by height in metres squared. Scored on the Asian Indian bands: healthy 18.5 to 22.9, overweight 23 to 24.9, obesity 25 and above. The WHO global category is shown alongside.

Belly fat. A waist of 90 cm or more for men, 80 cm or more for women, or a waist to height ratio above 0.5. The 2025 revised Indian definition of obesity treats BMI above 23 with excess belly fat as the more serious stage.

Readings. Blood pressure on ACC/AHA bands, fasting glucose and HbA1c on ADA cut offs, SGPT on gastroenterology healthy limits (33 U/L men, 25 U/L women).

The plan. Each start or stop row is triggered by your numbers: activity under 150 minutes, steps under 7,000, sleep under 7 hours, sitting 6 hours or more, sugary drinks, or a flagged reading. Activity targets follow WHO guidance.

Not medical advice. This tool is for education and habit building. It does not diagnose anything. Talk to a doctor about any flagged reading, and get care the same day for blood pressure of 180 / 120 or more.

FAQ

### Common Questions

What is a healthy BMI for Indians? For Asian Indian adults the healthy range is 18.5 to 22.9. A BMI of 23 to 24.9 counts as overweight and 25 or above as obesity. These cut offs are lower than the WHO global ones (25 and 30) because Indians develop diabetes and heart disease at lower body weight, which is why Indian doctors use them.
How do I calculate BMI? BMI is your weight in kilograms divided by your height in metres squared. At 170 cm and 72 kg that is 72 ÷ (1.7 × 1.7) = 24.9. The calculator does this for you and shows the weight range that is healthy for your height.
Why does waist size matter as much as BMI? Fat around the belly drives insulin resistance, fatty liver and heart risk, and Indians carry more of it at the same BMI. The 2025 revised Indian definition of obesity uses BMI above 23 together with a waist of 90 cm or more for men, 80 cm or more for women, or a waist to height ratio above 0.5.
What blood pressure, sugar and SGPT readings are normal? Blood pressure under 120 / 80 is normal and 130 / 80 or more is high. Fasting glucose under 100 mg/dL and HbA1c under 5.7% are normal, with 100 to 125 and 5.7 to 6.4% in the prediabetes range. For SGPT (ALT), gastroenterology guidance puts the healthy upper limit near 33 U/L for men and 25 U/L for women, though many labs print 40. Your doctor reads these with your full history.
How much weight should I aim to lose first? Five to seven percent of your current weight over six months. For a 78 kg adult that is about 4 to 5.5 kg. Losses of this size measurably lower blood pressure, blood sugar and liver fat, even before you reach the healthy BMI range.
Is my data saved or shared? No. Everything runs in your browser. Health readings never go into the share link. Habit ticks are saved only on this device and reset every Monday. The PDF is built on your device.

References: Misra A et al., Revised definition of obesity in Asian Indians living in India, Diabetes and Metabolic Syndrome, 2025; WHO guidelines on physical activity, 2020; ACC/AHA blood pressure guideline, 2017; ADA Standards of Care; ACG clinical guideline on abnormal liver chemistries, 2017. This calculator is for education only and is not a substitute for medical advice.

Guide

### How Do You Calculate BMI for Indians?

Quick answer BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. For Asian Indian adults the healthy range is 18.5 to 22.9, 23 to 24.9 is overweight and 25 or more is obesity. These cut offs are lower than the global WHO scale because health risk starts at a lower BMI in Indians.

#### How to use it

- Enter height and weight Height in centimetres and weight in kilograms, measured in the morning.
- Add your waist Measure at the navel. Waist size flags belly fat that BMI can miss.
- Fill your daily habits Steps, cardio, sleep, sitting time and food. These drive the start and stop table.
- Get your plan Read the insights, track 8 habits for 7 days and download the PDF plan.

#### The formula
BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²
Waist to height ratio = waist (cm) ÷ height (cm)

#### Worked example
170 cm and 78 kg: 78 ÷ 1.70² = 27.0. On Indian cut offs that is in the obesity band, while the WHO global scale calls it overweight. The healthy weight for 170 cm on Indian cut offs is about 53 to 66 kg.

#### More questions people ask

##### What is a normal BMI for Indian adults?
18.5 to 22.9 on the Asian Indian cut offs used by Indian guidelines. The global WHO scale uses 18.5 to 24.9.

##### Why is the BMI cut off lower for Indians?
At the same BMI, Indians tend to carry more body fat and belly fat, which raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease earlier. Lower cut offs catch that risk sooner.

##### Is waist size more important than BMI?
Both matter. A waist of 90 cm or more for men, or 80 cm or more for women, or a waist to height ratio above 0.5, signals belly fat even when BMI looks normal.

##### How many steps a day should I walk?
Around 7,000 to 10,000 steps a day is linked with lower health risk in large studies. Start from your current count and add about 1,000 a week.
